name: Vermentino

lines.s10: Vermentino is the white of the Mediterranean coast: lime, green apple and wild fennel, with a salty, faintly bitter almond finish.
lines.s20: Vermentino grows within sight of the sea, from Sardinia and Corsica to Liguria and Provence. It is dry and crisp, with lime, green apple and wild fennel, and it finishes on a pinch of salt and a twist of bitter almond.
lines.s45: Vermentino lives by the sea. Its home is Sardinia, above all the granite hills of Gallura, and it follows the coast through Corsica, Liguria and Tuscany to Provence, where it is called Rolle. It tastes of lime, green apple and white peach, with a scent of wild fennel. It is dry and medium bodied, and it finishes on salt and a touch of bitter almond. Most of it is made cold in steel and sold young, with no oak. Pour it with grilled fish, shellfish or anything with pesto. In Liguria the same grape, with freckled skins, goes by the name Pigato.
lines.sale: Vermentino is the seaside white: lime, wild fennel and a salty snap that makes fish taste fresher. I would pour it with the grilled fish or the oysters, as you would squeeze a lemon over them.

glass.lead: Lime, green apple and white peach with wild fennel, crisp and medium bodied, finishing salty with a twist of bitter almond.

ladder.where: Liguria and the Colli di Luni, cooled by sea breezes
Sardinia, Corsica, the Tuscan Maremma, Provence and McLaren Vale

glass.structure: Dry. Acidity medium to medium plus, alcohol medium, body medium, with a salty, faintly bitter finish.

home.home: Sardinia first, where Vermentino di Gallura on windy granite is the island's only DOCG, then Corsica, Liguria, the Tuscan coast, Provence and the Languedoc. Nearly all of it is fermented cool in steel and bottled young, sometimes rested on its lees for weight: crisp, salty and scented with wild fennel.
home.abroad: Australia has taken to it, in McLaren Vale, the Riverland and the King Valley, and California bottles a little. Both keep to the home style: lime and grapefruit, firm acidity and no oak, a touch riper from warm sites.

service.temp: 45 to 50 degrees Fahrenheit, 7 to 10 degrees Celsius: cold, but not so cold that the scent closes.
service.glass: A white wine glass, tapered to hold the scent.
service.decant: Unnecessary; open it cold and pour.
service.age: Enjoy it young, within two or three years; a Gallura Superiore holds a little longer.

with.dish: Grilled whole fish with lemon and olive oil
with.why: its acidity and salt act like the lemon
a crisp, salty white mirrors the brine

with.dish: Fried calamari or small fried fish
with.why: crisp acidity cuts through the frying

labels.means: Sardinia's only DOCG: at least 95 per cent Vermentino from the granite north east; Superiore is fuller.
The grape's name in Provence and the Languedoc; a little also goes into Provence rosé.
The same grape by DNA on Liguria's western coast, bottled under its own name; fuller and more savoury.
The Corsican name, on the whites of Patrimonio, Ajaccio and the island's other appellations.

guest.q: Is Rolle the same as Vermentino?
guest.a: Yes. Rolle is what Provence and the Languedoc call it, Vermentinu is the Corsican name, and Liguria's Pigato is the same grape too. The wine is dry, crisp and a little salty wherever it grows.

guest.q: I like Sauvignon Blanc. Will I like this?
guest.a: I think so. It is as crisp and dry, but quieter: lime and green apple in place of cut grass and passion fruit, with a salty, slightly bitter almond finish.
Nobody can say for certain. The vines grow in sea wind on poor, stony ground, and the wine has a briny edge that sits well with fish and shellfish.

compare.tell: Albariño has more peach and apricot, higher acidity and no almond; Vermentino smells of wild fennel and ends on a twist of bitter almond.
Sauvignon Blanc is louder and greener, with cut grass, gooseberry and passion fruit; Vermentino is quieter, saltier and ends on bitter almond.
Italian Pinot Grigio is more neutral, with pear and little scent; Vermentino has more lime, wild fennel and salt.

cards.front: Vermentino: what is Sardinia's only DOCG, and what is the ground?
cards.back: Vermentino di Gallura, raised to DOCG in 1996: at least 95 per cent Vermentino from the windy granite of the island's north east.

cards.front: Vermentino: what is it called in Provence, in Corsica and in Liguria?
cards.back: Rolle in Provence and the Languedoc, Vermentinu in Corsica, and Pigato on Liguria's western coast, where it is grown and bottled as a vine of its own.

cards.front: Vermentino blind: which finish parts it from Sauvignon Blanc and Albariño?
cards.back: A salty edge and a twist of bitter almond, on a quieter scent of lime, green apple and wild fennel, with medium body and no oak.

questions.q: A blind white is pale straw, dry, crisp and unoaked, with lime, green apple and wild fennel, a salty edge and a faint bitter almond finish. Which grape is it most likely to be?
questions.exp: A quiet scent of lime and wild fennel, a salty edge and a bitter almond finish point to Vermentino. Albariño shows more peach and apricot and higher acidity, with no almond.

questions.q: A guest in Nice is poured a white Bellet made from Rolle and asks what that grape is called in Italy. What do you answer?
questions.exp: Rolle is the Provençal name of Vermentino and the main white grape of Bellet, above Nice. Trebbiano grows in Provence too, as Ugni Blanc, but it is a different grape.

questions.q: A guest asks for the Sardinian white of the island's top legal rank to go with her grilled fish. Which wine do you bring?
questions.exp: Vermentino di Gallura, from the granite north east, is Sardinia's only DOCG. Vermentino di Sardegna is the lighter DOC made across the whole island.

No Codex record on Vermentino is believed wrong. Gallura as Sardinia's only DOCG (1996, at least 95 per cent), Pigato as Vermentino by DNA with freckled skins, Vermentinu in Corsica, Rolle in Provence and at Bellet, and the cool steel cellar all stand on the Codex's own region records.

The rule that French labels may no longer say Vermentino from the 2022 harvest stands on two trade reports of 2022 (The Drinks Business and Meininger). It is a rule that could be changed: a checker should confirm it still stands before it ships, and strike the second half of the Rolle label row if not.

Vermentino di Gallura as the only DOCG of Sardinia (1996, at least 95 per cent), Pigato and Favorita as the same vine by DNA, Vermentinu and Rolle, Rolle as the main white grape of Bellet, and McLaren Vale, the Riverland and the King Valley abroad were confirmed.
